# Religion Dictionary
## B [▲](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#startofdictionary)
**[Baha'i](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=97)**: A [religion](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religion) started in 19th century Persia (now Iran) by Mirza Husain Ali. The Baha'i faith is now worldwide and teaches the unity of God, the truth of his [prophets](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Prophet), and continuation of revelation in every age. It has no priesthood, believing in spiritual equality between men and women (Parrinder 1973: 39).

**Baptism**: The rite of applying water to a person, usually marking his or her entrance into the [Christian church](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity). It appears to have derived from John the Baptist in the first century CE, although some scholars believe that the act was inspired by the ritual ablution of the Jewish Essenes. [Churches](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Church) and [denominations](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Denomination) are divided on whether baptism literally or symbolically washes away [sin](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sin) (Smith and Green 1995: 102-103).

**Baptist**: Protestants that originated from 17th century English Puritanism. The term "Baptist" came from their insistence that [baptism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Baptism) should be reserved for those old enough to comprehend and confess a personal faith in [Jesus](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ). Modern Baptist churches teach that only believers should be voluntarily baptized by immersion (Reid et al. 1990: 110). For more on the Baptist family, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=96). To interactively explore the history of Baptists in America, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/interactive-display?tid=6).

**Bar Mitzvah**: This [Jewish](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=106) ceremony, usually performed when a boy is 13, marks his passage into adulthood. The ceremony includes a reading from the [Torah](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Torah) or the Prophets, and is followed by an elaborate party for friends and family (Smith and Green 1995: 104).

**Bat Mitzvah**: A [Jewish](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=106) ceremony, usually performed when a girl is 12, which marks her transition into adulthood. The ceremony includes a reading from the [Torah](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Torah) or the [Prophets](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Prophet), and is followed by an elaborate party for friends and family. The Bat Mitzvah is a fairly new rite of passage in modern times, and functions as a way to give the girl more of a role in Jewish public life (Hinnells 1984: 37).

**Belief in "End Times," Measures of**: [Survey](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Survey) items [measuring](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Measure/Measurement) views toward certain religious predictions about the end of the world, such as [Armageddon](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Armageddon) and the [Rapture](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Rapture).

**Belief in Angels/Demons, Measures of**: These [survey](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Survey) item [measures](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Measure/Measurement) whether a respondent believes in [angels](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Angel) or [demons](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Demon). Examples of these items are found in the [2007 U.S. Religious Landscape Survey](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?fid=RELLAND) and the [2005 Baylor Religion Survey](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?fid=BRS2005), both available in the ARDA’s Data Archive.

**Belief in Creationism/Acceptance of Evolution, Measure of**: These [variables](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Variable) can be used to explore whether or not respondents believe in a [literal creation story](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Creationism) or if creation should be taught in schools and whether they accept versions of evolutionary theory presented by contemporary science. Examples of these measures are found in the [2008 General Social Survey](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?fid=GSS08PAN), [2007 U.S. Religious Landscape Survey](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?fid=RELLAND) and the [2005 Religion and Public Life Survey](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?fid=RELPUB05), all of which are available in the ARDA’s Data Archive.

**Belief in God, Measure of**: This [survey](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Survey) item assesses whether a respondent believes in [God](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#God/Goddess).

**Belief in Heaven, Measures of**: One’s views on the certainty of a positive [afterlife](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Afterlife) existing, or occasionally, questions about who will be allowed to go there. Examples of these [measures](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Measure/Measurement) are found in the [2008 General Social Survey](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?fid=GSS08PAN), [2005 Baylor Religion Survey](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?fid=BRS2005) and the [2005 National Study of Youth and Religion](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?fid=NSYRW2), all of which are available in the ARDA’s Data Archive.

**Belief in Hell, Measure of**: This [survey](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Survey) item assesses whether a respondent believes in [hell](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Hell%20(Christianity)) or [purgatory](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Purgatory).

**Belief in Jesus, Measure of**: This [survey](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Survey) item assesses what respondents believe about the [divinity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Divinity) (or lack thereof) regarding [Jesus](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ). Examples of this [measure](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Measure/Measurement) are present in the [2005 National Study of Youth and Religion](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?fid=NSYRW2) and the [2005 Baylor Religion Survey](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?fid=BRS2005), both of which are available in the ARDA’s Data Archive.

**Belief in Satan, Measure of**: This [survey](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Survey) item measures whether a respondent believes in [Satan/the devil](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Satan).

**Belief, Religious**: On its most basic level, religious belief refers to views toward the [supernatural](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Supernatural).

**Bhagavad Gita**: The most popular [scripture](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Scriptures) in contemporary [Hinduism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Hinduism).

**Bible, Christian**: The [sacred](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sacred) text for [Christians](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christians), comprising the [Old](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Old%20Testament%20(Hebrew%20Bible)) and [New Testaments](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#New%20Testament). The New Testament contains twenty-seven books: the four [Gospels](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Gospels) of [Jesus'](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ) life, the Acts of the Apostles, twenty-one letters, and the [Book of Revelation](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Book%20of%20Revelation). The [canon](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Canon) of the New Testament became official in the Easter Letter of Athanasius in 367 CE. It is important to note that Bibles in the [Roman Catholic](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=708) and [Eastern Orthodox churches](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=89) contain more books, including the [apocrypha](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Apocrypha) (Smith and Green 1995: 113).

**Bible, Hebrew (Tanakh)**: The [sacred](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sacred) text of [Judaism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Judaism), also known as the [Old Testament](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Old%20Testament%20(Hebrew%20Bible)) for [Christians](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christians).

**Biblical Inerrancy**: The belief that the [Bible](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Bible,%20Christian) is without error, in terms of [theology](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Theology), ethics, history, geography, and science. This is common in [Christian fundamentalism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Fundamentalism), as opposed to [evangelicals](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Evangelical%20Protestantism) who typically have a less strict view that the Bible, and instead simply believe that the Bible is the inspired word of God (Prothero 2008: 235).

**Biblical Literalism**: The extent to which individuals believe that the [Bible](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Bible,%20Christian) (or other sacred scriptures) should be interpreted literally.

**Bishop**: A senior [member](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Member) of the [clergy](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Clergy) who is in charge of a [diocese](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Diocese) or association of [congregations](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Congregation) or [parishes](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Parish) (Smith and Green 1995: 116).

**Black Muslims**: [Members](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Member) of the Nation of Islam. See [Nation of Islam](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Nation%20of%20Islam) for more.

**[Black Protestantism](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/traditions?T=6)**: Also known as the Black Church, Black Protestantism is a unique [religious tradition](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religious%20Tradition%20(RELTRAD)) that has theological and structural similarities to white [evangelical](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Evangelical%20Protestantism) [denominations](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Denomination), but also emphasizes social justice and community activism. Black Protestants tend to be liberal on economic issues, but conservative on social issues. Historically, seven major denominations compose this religious tradition, including the [African Methodist Episcopal Church](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=177), the [Church of God in Christ](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=74), and the [Progressive National Baptist Convention](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=40). For more information, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/traditions?T=6).

**Black Theology**: A system of Christian thought that focuses on [God](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#God/Goddess) as a liberator of the oppressed, specifically those in the black community. It derives from traditional African-American religion and [liberation theology](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Liberation%20Theology). Many attribute its development to the Civil Rights and Black Power movements of the 1950s/1960s (Reid et al. 1990: 161-164).

**Blasphemy**: An act or verbal offense that mocks beliefs, sacred beings, or objects in a certain religion. In some religions, like [Islam](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Islam), blasphemy and [heresy](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Heresy) are sometimes used interchangeably (Smith and Green 1995: 118).

**Blood Transfusions and Jehovah’s Witnesses**: It is a common practice for [Jehovah’s Witnesses](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=450) (JW) to refuse blood transfusions, even in life or death situations, on religious grounds. JW believe that one should not sustain one’s life with the blood or another creature, whether through drinking blood or taking someone else’s blood directly into their blood vessels. In this way, JW believe that Jehovah (God) condemns blood transfusions and will condemn those who receive them. Although refusal among adults is accepted as one’s right to personal freedom, the refusal of blood transfusions for JW children is more controversial (Swan 1997). JW have typically lost legal cases involving the health of children (Koenig, King and Carson 2012: 65).

**Bodhisattva (Bodhissata)**: One destined for [enlightenment](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Enlightenment) in the [Buddhist](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Buddhism) tradition. In [Theravada Buddhism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Theravada%20Buddhism), it is one on the way to becoming a Buddha. In [Mahayana Buddhism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Mahayana%20Buddhism), there are many Bodhisattvas, and they function as embodiments of ideals like compassion. One of the greatest bodhisattvas in Mahayana Buddhism is Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion (Parrinder 1973: 48).

**Book of Mormon**: The [sacred](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sacred) text of [Latter-day Saints (Mormons)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=211), along with the [Bible](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Bible,%20Christian). It is said that the angel [Moroni](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Moroni) led church founder [Joseph Smith](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=43) to golden plates in 1827. According to Smith, the [angel](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Angel) gave him gold plates that were engraved in what Smith describes as a reformed Egyptian language. The angel also gave him two divining stones, the Urim and Thummim, which were used to translate the text. The Book of Mormon tells the story of two groups of people: the Jeradites and the Israelites. In the book, [Jesus](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ) visits the New World after his resurrection and before his ascension. Smith also received other revelations, including the _Book of Moses_, the _Book of Abraham_, and an alternate translation of the Bible (Melton 2009: 635-636).

**Book of Revelation**: An important book in [Christian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) [apocalypticism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Apocalypse) and [millenarianism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Millenarianism). It is the last book in the [New Testament](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#New%20Testament) [canon](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Canon), and it is written by John of Patmos. The book deals with the [end-times](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#End-Times) as well as persecution by the Roman government at the time.

**Born-Again**: A term used by [Jesus](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ) in the New Testament that is now employed to describe the conversion experience for many [evangelical](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Evangelical%20Protestantism) and [fundamentalist](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Fundamentalism) Christians.

**Brahman**: A [Hindu](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Hinduism) concept referring to the world spirit that arises at creation. Hindus believe that it is either in an impersonal form (Nirguna Brahman) or human form (Saguna Brahman) (Esposito et al. 2012a: G-4).

**Brain Drain (Religion)**: In the context of [religion](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religion), it refers to the departure of highly productive/skilled members from [religious groups](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religious%20Group).

**Brainwashing**: This controversial term refers to the possibility that coercive or deceptive indoctrination techniques can take control over a person’s mind; for example, causing the individual to join a radical [new religious movement](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#New%20Religious%20Movements) (i.e. [“cult”](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Cult)).

**Branch Davidians**: A breakaway [Christian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) [Adventist](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=98) group that was infamously sieged by the U.S. government in 1993 at Mt. Carmel Center, the Davidians' compund outside Waco, Texas. The Branch Davidians began as an offshoot of the Davidian Seventh-day Adventist Association in 1930. After a divisive fight in the 1950s, Vernon Howell, who later assumed the messianic name of [David Koresh](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Koresh,%20David%20(1958-1993)), became the prominent leader of the group. That set off a siege of nearly two months. Carmel. A fire erupted, the complex burned down and many members died, including David Koresh (Smith and Green 1995: 127-128).

1998). 2012: 94-120).

**[Brownson, Orestes (1803-1876)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=58)**: Orestes Brownson (1803-1876) was a 19th century public intellectual in the United States. He defended [Catholicism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Catholicism,%20Roman) and its compatibility with American society, which was controversial at the time, for Catholics were a small minority that many [Protestant](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Protestantism) Americans viewed with skepticism. For more on Orestes Brownson, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=58).

**Buddha**: It literally means one who has "awakened," reaching [enlightenment](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Enlightenment) and escaping rebirth (see [samsara](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Samsara)). This also is the name given to [Siddhartha Gautama](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Siddhartha%20Gautama), the founder of the [Buddhist religion](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Buddhism) (Esposito et al. 2012a: G-6).

**Buddha-nature**: The inborn essence of all sentient beings that enable them with the potential for Buddhahood. This is a prominent belief in Chinese [Buddhism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Buddhism) (Smith and Green 1995: 129).

**Buddhism**: A world religion founded by [Siddhartha Gautama](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Siddhartha%20Gautama), the Buddha in the sixth or fifth century BCE in India. Teaching [reincarnation](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Reincarnation) and freedom from worldly attachments, Buddhism has three major branches: [Theravada](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Theravada%20Buddhism), [Mahayana](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Mahayana%20Buddhism) and [Vajrayana](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Tantric%20(Vajrayana)%20Buddhism). According to Buddhism, the origin of suffering comes from ignorance, and that one must follow the [Eightfold Path](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Eightfold%20Path) to reach [nirvana](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Nirvana). Buddhism first came to America through Chinese immigration (Prothero 2008: 205-206).

**Buddhist**: An [adherent](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Adherent) of [Buddhism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Buddhism).

In the religious realm, as new churches are started, new [denominations](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Denomination) emerge and the parachurch sector continues to grow, bureaucracy is a way to study the trajectory of these organizations as they develop from an idea to a fully functioning organization (Weber 1946).

**Burka (Burqa)**: The garment that covers a [Muslim](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Muslim) woman's entire body (Esposito 2011: 242).

## C [▲](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#startofdictionary)
**Caliph**: A title for the political leader of the [Muslim](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Muslim) community. [Sunni](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sunni%20Islam) Muslims believe that the most qualified person should be elected as a caliph, whereas [Shi'ite](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Shi'ite%20Islam) Muslims believe that the caliph should come from the bloodline of [Ali](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Ali), [Muhammad's](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Muhammad%20(Mohammad)) cousin and son-in-law (Esposito 2011: 43).

**Calvinism**: Also known as Reformed [theology](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Theology), Calvinism is a [Protestant](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Protestantism) theological tradition based on the works of John Calvin (1509-1564). Calvin believed in the absolute sovereignty of God and the total depravity of humans. Calvinism also includes the doctrine of double [predestination](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Predestination): the belief that God fated every human being, before birth, to either [heaven](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Heaven%20(Christianity)) or [hell](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Hell%20(Christianity)) (Prothero 2008: 207).

**[Cane Ridge Camp Meeting](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=239)**: Barton Stone organized the Cane Ridge camp meeting (1801), the largest and most famous [religious revival](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Revival,%20Religious) of the [Second Great Awakening](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=326). It took place in Bourbon County, Kentucky, and he invited [Presbyterian](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/family-trees?F=91), [Baptist](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Baptist) and [Methodist](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Methodist-Pietist%20Family) preachers. For more information on Cane Ridge Camp Meeting, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=239).

**Canon**: A general term for an authoritative set of [sacred](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sacred) texts (Smith and Green 1995: 179).

**Canon Law**: [Church](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Church) law or decrees given by an ecclesiastical authority for governing a given church. In [Roman Catholicism](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=708), there is a history of systematic collections dating back to the 11th century, but the first code of canon law was promulgated in 1917, and was revised several times since its inception. It includes the obligations of the [clergy](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Clergy) and [laity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Laity), [missionary activities](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Mission/Missionary%20Movements), Catholic education, [worship](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Worship%20(Christianity)) and the [sacraments](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sacrament) (Reid et al. 1990: 219-220).

**Cardinal**: A papal-appointed position in the [Roman Catholic Church](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=708) responsible for electing new [popes](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Pope). The term originally applied to all [clergy](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Clergy) with permanent positions. Currently, there are more than 100 cardinals (Reid et al. 1990: 223).

**[Carroll, John (1735-1815)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=130)**: John Carroll served as the first [Catholic](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Catholicism,%20Roman) [bishop](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Bishop) in the United States and helped expand the Catholic Church domestically. For more information on John Carroll, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=130).

**Catechism**: A manual of instruction in the basics of the [Christian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) faith. Examples of catechisms include Luther's German catechism (1529) and the Roman Catechism (1566).

**Cathedral**: A building traditionally designated as the principal [church](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Church) of a [diocese](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Diocese) or [archdiocese](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Archdiocese) in the [Catholic](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=87), [Anglican](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=88) and [Orthodox](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=89) traditions (Reid et al. 1990: 232).

**[Catholic Church Abuse Scandal](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=313)**: The [Catholic Church](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Catholicism,%20Roman) abuse scandal involves widespread allegations of child sexual abuse at the hands of Catholic [clergy](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Clergy) and institutional cover-ups by Catholic officials. For more information on the abuse scandal, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=313).

**[Catholic Worker Movement](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=325)**: A [Catholic](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Catholicism,%20Roman) movement created to serve the poor. It was founded by [Dorothy Day](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=68) and [Peter Maurin](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=69) during the [Great Depression](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=297), and it still exists today. For more information, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=325).

**Catholicism, Roman**: The largest of [Christianity's](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) three main branches, which include the [Eastern Orthodox Church](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=89) and [Protestantism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Protestantism). Catholicism maintains a hierarchy of [bishops](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Bishop) and [priests](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Priest), with the [pope](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Pope) as the clerical leader. Notable differences from Protestantism also include the veneration of the Virgin Mary and other saints, the importance of church traditions, and the [celibacy](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Celibacy) of the priesthood (Prothero 2008: 208). For more information on the Roman Catholic Church, including membership data, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=708). To interactively explore the history of Catholics in America, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/interactive-display?tid=7).

**Celibacy**: The renunciation of marriage and sexual relations as part of a religious vocation. [Roman Catholic](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=708) [priests](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Priest) are celibate while [Orthodox](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=89) priests are not required to be celibate (Smith and Green 1995: 190-191).

**Charisma**: Often distinguished by two very broad meanings: (1) possessing a [divine](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Divinity) gift, and (2) having the charm to inspire devotion in the minds of other people.

**Charisma of Minister, Measure of**: This [survey](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Survey) item asks respondents if the reason they attended or joined a [religious group](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religious%20Group) was due to the charisma of a [minister](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Minister).

**Charismatics**: [Christians](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christians) who stress spiritual gifts described in the [New Testament](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#New%20Testament), such as [speaking in tongues](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Speaking%20In%20Tongues) and healing. Prior to 1960, this phenomenon was closely associated with the [Pentecostal](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=94) tradition (see [Azusa Street Revival](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=211)), but since then it has become a more general term that emphasizes the presence of the [Holy Spirit](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Holy%20Spirit), without a specific denominational affiliation (Smith and Green 1995: 194).

Examples of this [measure](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Measure/Measurement) are found in the [2008 General Social Survey](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?fid=GSS08PAN), [2005 Baylor Religion Survey](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?fid=BRS2005) and the [1998 General Social Survey](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?fid=GSS1998), all available in the ARDA’s Data Archive.

**Childhood Religious Identity, Measure of**: A [survey](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Survey) [measure](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Measure/Measurement) of an individual’s religious affiliation or salience as a child.

**Christian Apocrypha**: Also known as the [New Testament](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#New%20Testament) Apocrypha, it is a collection of non-canonical [Christian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) writings purporting to contain information regarding [Jesus](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ) and other first-century Christian leaders. Books in the Christian Apocrypha include the Gospel of Thomas and the Gospel of Peter. The major branches of Christianity do not view these books as authoritative, as many of them were written much later than the [New Testament](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#New%20Testament) [canon](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Canon). The Christian Apocrypha is different from the Old Testament [Apocrypha](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Apocrypha), or deuterocanonical books (Smith and Green 1995: 55).

**Christian Coalition**: A conservative political pressure group composed of white [evangelicals](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Evangelical%20Protestantism) and [Catholics](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=87) that was established in 1989 by [Pat Robertson](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=17) after he failed to receive the Republican nomination in the presidential election. The Christian Coalition is the spiritual successor to [Jerry Falwell's](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=18) [Moral Majority of the 1980s](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=46). Today, the group is known for promoting "family values" and a return to the nation's "Christian heritage" (Prothero 2008: 209).

**Christian Science Family**: Churches following the teachings of founder [Mary Baker Eddy (1821-1910)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=135), who believed that personal healing was the central message of [Christianity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity). She believed that the correct interpretation of Scripture would alleviate disease, suffering, and even death according to her book _Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures_ (1875). The movement became more of an institution in 1879. [Worship](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Worship%20(Christianity)) services include readings from the [Bible](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Bible,%20Christian) as well as Eddy's "Science and Health." The largest group in the [Christian Science family](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=102) is the [Church of Christ, Scientist](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=186) (Smith and Green 1995: 264).

**Christianity**: The largest of the world [religions](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religion), comprising a third of the world's population. The three main branches of Christianity are [Eastern Orthodoxy](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=89), [Roman Catholicism](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=708), and [Protestantism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Protestantism) (Prothero 2008: 209-210). See the ARDA's [American Denomination: Profiles](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups) web page for specific [denominations](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Denomination) of Christianity.

**Christians**: [Adherents](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Adherent) of the Christian religion. See [Christianity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) for more details.

**Christmas**: A [Christian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) holiday generally celebrated on December 25th that commemorates the birth of [Jesus Christ](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ). Some [Orthodox](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=89) Christians celebrate Christmas on January 7th (Prothero 2008: 210).

**Christology**: The [theological](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Theology) study of [Jesus Christ](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ), mostly concerned with his person and nature (Reid et al. 1990: 263).

**Church**: 1) A building, program or service providing religious goods to a certain constituency and a specific geographical location. 2) Historically and [theologically](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Theology), it represents a [Christian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) community founded on the teachings of [Jesus Christ](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ) (Reid et al. 1990: 266).

**Church/Sect Cycle**: A cycle whereby new religious bodies begin as [sects](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sect) that have high [tension](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Tension) with their surrounding environment and gradually transform into [churches](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Church) that have low tension with their surrounding environment.

**Churches as Firms**: Churches may operate as “firms,” seeking to market their product to potential clients and “franchise” into new territories. For example, Finke and Stark (1992) explain the explosive growth of Methodist and Baptist churches in 19th century America to superior marketing, organization and [clergy](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Clergy) incentives (Iannaccone and Berman 2018).

**Circumcision**: In [Judaism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Judaism), the cutting of the penis's foreskin as a sign of the covenant between God and [Abraham's](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Abraham) offspring. The practice is also common among [Christians](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christians) and [Muslims](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Muslim), along with some indigenous groups (Esposito et al. 2012b: G-4).

**Civic Engagement**: This refers to individuals’ levels of participation in civic society (public sphere).

**Civil Religion**: A religio-political phenomenon describing the general faith of a nation or state, and its commonly held beliefs about the history and destiny of the nation. The term was coined by Jean-Jacques Rousseau in his book, _Social Contract_ (1762). 1990: 281).

**Civilization Theory**: Theories in this broad category assert that each major civilization, and perhaps smaller units as well in prehistoric times and remote regions, has a degree of cultural coherence, often marked by a distinctive [religion](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religion).

**Clergy**: [Ordained](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Ordination) leaders who carry out religious duties. [Roman Catholic](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=708), [Eastern Orthodox](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=89), and [Anglican churches](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=88) tend to emphasize the distinction between the clergy and the [laity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Laity), although this distinction exists in various other [Protestant](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Protestantism) denominations to a lesser degree (Reid et al. 1990: 293).

**Club Models of Religion**: Club models of [religion](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religion) emphasize how effective [congregations](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Congregation) function more like families or social clubs rather than [firms](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Churches%20as%20Firms). Club models have made major contributions to our understanding of high-demanding [‘cults’](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Cult), [‘sects’](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sect) and [religious extremism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religious%20Extremism), as studies have found substantially higher levels of mutual aid and social cohesion in more sectarian religious communities (Iannacconne and Berman 2018).

**Cognitive Theories**: Cognitive theories of religion seek to integrate the scientific study of the mind, intelligence and cognition into explanations of religious belief. Several cognitive theories of religious phenomena include [attribution of intentionality](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Attribution%20of%20Intentionality), [cognitive consistency](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Cognitive%20Consistency), [cognitive efficiency](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Cognitive%20Efficiency), [modes of memory](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Modes%20of%20Memory) and [pragmatic epistemology](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Pragmatic%20Epistemology).

**[Communal Family](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=101)**: [Churches](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Church) where [members](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Member) often live together or share living activities, such as common meals, as an expression of their faith. The [Hutterian Brethren](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=412) is an example of a communal church (Smith and Green 1995: 275).

**Communes, Religious**: Communities that share beliefs and possessions while striving internally for equality. The [Shakers](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=863) were fairly successful in maintaining communes in the 18th and 19th century.

**Communion**: 1) The [Christian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) commemoration of [Christ's](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ) last supper by partaking of the elements of bread and wine (or grape juice). Communion also is known as the [Eucharist](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Eucharist) in some Christian traditions. 2) The fellowship of all Christians on earth and in heaven. 3) A specific Christian church or family of churches (Hinnells 1984: 94).

**Complementary and Alternative Medicine (CAM) Scale**: Health care approaches developed outside of mainstream Western, or conventional, medicine (National Institutes of Health 2018). When used in conjunction with conventional medicine, it’s considered “complementary,” but when used as a replacement for conventional medicine, it’s considered “alternative.” Historically and in modern times, spiritual practices may function as CAM treatments, as [prayer](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Prayer) remains the most common practice used for healing (P.M. Barnes et al. 2004).

**Confession**: A [sacrament](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sacrament) in the [Roman Catholic](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=708) and [Orthodox](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=89) churches in which a penitent confesses his or her [sins](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sin) to a [priest](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Priest) and is absolved of them. In Roman Catholicism, confession is only one part of the entire sacrament of penance (Smith and Green 1995: 280).

Confirmation is most often celebrated in the [Roman Catholic](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=708), [Episcopal](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=88), [Lutheran](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=90), [Methodist](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=92) and [Presbyterian](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=91) denominations (Smith and Green 1995: 280).

**Confucianism**: A Chinese [religion](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religion) founded by Confucius (551-479 BCE), whose goal was to foster social harmony through a combination of self-cultivation and social rites. Chinese Immigrants brought Confucianism to the United States in the 19th century (Prothero 2008: 211-212).

**Confucius (551-479 BCE)**: A Chinese philosopher who taught concepts of righteousness and of "being fully human." His [disciples](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Disciple) helped spread his philosophy, which later became known as [Confucianism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Confucianism) in the Han dynasty. His name actually was Master K'ung, but [Catholic](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=708) [missionaries](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Mission/Missionary%20Movements) later referred to him as Confucius, a Latinized version of his name (Esposito et al. 2012: 491-492).

**Congregation**: Any local gathering of believers for worship. This can be thought of as a more inclusive term for [church](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Church), since many religious traditions use different names for their place of worship. Usually this refers to a building or physical structure, but it also could refer to a more fluid group of people without a specific building (e.g. a 'congregation' that meets in member's homes).

**Congregationalism**: A system of [church](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Church) governance in which the [members](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Member) hold most of the power, such as electing the [clergy](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Clergy) and making other major decisions. 2) Congregationalism can also refer to the church tradition stemming from the English Puritans of the 17th century and now found in the United States in the United Church of Christ and smaller Congregationalist bodies (Smith and Green 1995: 285-286).

**Conservative Judaism**: An offshoot of [Reform Judaism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Reform%20Judaism) in America that officially began in the early 20th century, but traces its early thought pattern to European [Jews](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jews) in the mid-19th century.

**Conservative Protestantism**: A broad social category of [Protestantism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Protestantism) that advocates a conservative theological position (e.g., the inspiration of the [Bible](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Bible,%20Christian), the physical resurrection of [Jesus Christ](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ), etc.). Conservative Protestants are often subdivided into [Evangelical Protestants](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Evangelical%20Protestantism) and [Fundamentalists](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Fundamentalism), who differ in terms of their engagement with the [secular](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Secular) non-Christian world.

**Control Theory**: Control theory, as originally formulated by Travis Hirschi (1969), posited that group member behavior is regulated by four aspects of social bondedness: attachment, commitment, involvement and belief.

In [Christianity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity), it is a turning away from [sin](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sin) and toward a new life of [Christ](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ). 1990: 316). Some [sociologists of religion](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sociology%20of%20Religion) define conversion as the shift in religious allegiance from one religious tradition to another, from [Judaism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Judaism) to Christianity, for example. These scholars would define the shift from the [Baptist](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=96) to the [Catholic](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=708) tradition as a process of [reaffiliation](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Reaffiliation), not conversion (Stark and Finke 2000: 114).

Examples of this [measure](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Measure/Measurement) are found in the [2005 Baylor Religion Survey](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?fid=BRS2005) and the [2001 U.S. Congregational Life Survey](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive/browse-categories?cid=C-B-A-C#C-B-A-C), both of which are available in the ARDA’s Data Archive.

**Conversion Theory**: Inspired by Lofland’s field research on recruitment to the [Unification Church](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Unification%20Church), Conversion Theory offers a series of steps a person must go through in order to become a member of a [new religious](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#New%20Religious%20Movements) [group](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religious%20Group): 1) experience enduring, acutely felt tensions within a religious problem-solving perspective, which leads him to define himself as a religious seeker; 2) encountering the group at a turning point in his/her life, wherein an affective bond is formed (or pre-exists) with one or more converts; 3) where extra- [cult](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Cult) attachments are absent or neutralized; 4) and where, if he is to become a deployable agent, he is exposed to intensive interaction (Lofland and Stark 1965).

**Conversion Therapy**: Conversion therapy is the controversial practice of converting homosexuals into heterosexuals (Hood, Hill and Spika 2009). Many conservative religionists believe that conversion therapy is effective (Haldeman 1994). Two-thirds of the clients were religious. Half of the 13 percent “success” stories experienced relapses.

For example, individuals may ask themselves, “What are the benefits/costs to me to believe in salvation?” (McCleary 2011).

**[Coughlin, Charles (1891-1979)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=74)**: Charles Coughlin was a [Catholic](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Catholicism,%20Roman) "radio [priest](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Priest)," who was controversial for his [anti-Semitic](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Anti-Semitism), pro-Nazi views leading up to World War II. For more information on Charles Coughlin, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=74).

**Counseling, Religious**: A type of counseling that incorporates religious teachings to serve [mental health needs](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Mental%20Health). Depending on the particular faith group, counseling may incorporate [prayer](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Prayer), [meditation](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Mediation) or [scripture](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Scriptures) reading.

**Creationism**: The belief that the creation account of Genesis, the first book of the Bible, is historically and scientifically correct.

Creeds are especially prominent in liturgical traditions. Some groups, like those in the [Restoration Movement](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/family-trees?F=115), state that there is "no creed, but Christ." [Baptist](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=96) groups also resist creedal statements. The most famous creeds are [Christianity's](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) [Apostles' Creed](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Apostles'%20Creed) and [Nicene Creed](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Nicene%20Creed) (Reid et al. 1990: 327).

**[Crosby, Frances "Fanny" (1820-1915)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=83)**: Fanny Crosby was a blind Christian [hymn](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Hymn) writer who wrote thousands of famous hymns, including "Blessed Assurance," "Jesus Keep Me Near the Cross," and "To God Be the Glory." For more information on Fanny Crosby, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=83).

**Cross**: 1) A sign widely used in the history of religion to express the structure of the cosmos. 2) An instrument of execution used by the Romans. 3) A [Christian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) symbol of salvation and God's compassion on humanity by allowing his Son, [Jesus Christ](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ), to die for humanity's sins (Smith and Green 1995: 297).

**Crucifix**: A cross bearing the figure of [Christ](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ). 1990: 330).

**Crusades**: Medieval military campaigns of the eleventh through fifteenth centuries waged by [Christians](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christians) to recapture [Jerusalem](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jerusalem) from [Muslims](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Muslim) (Prothero 2008: 214).

**Cult**: 1) A new and unconventional religious movement that is often founded on the teachings of a new prophet and/or new [sacred](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sacred) text. 2) The ARDA and other scholars tend to use the term ["new religious movements"](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#New%20Religious%20Movements) rather than cults because the latter term carries negative political and social connotations and prejudices associated with those belonging to such groups. 3) In popular use, people often refer to [sects](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sect) as cults (Smith and Green 1995: 298).

**Cultural Theories of Religion**: Theories of religion that examine how religious institutions, communities and symbols are embodied and connected to other aspects of society.

In most [Protestant](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Protestantism) churches, deacons are not [ordained](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Ordination) and are seen as people who assist the [clergy](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Clergy) (Reid et al. 1990: 344).

Deists believe in one God and in an [afterlife](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Afterlife) of rewards and punishments, but they reject both [miracles](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Miracle) and [prayers](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Prayer).

**Deity**: Typically, a [supernatural](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Supernatural) being considered holy or [sacred](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sacred).

**Delinquency/Crime, and Religion**: Problem behavior, usually by the young, that is either against the basic principles of society or is harmful to society or is in violation of the law (Koenig et al. 2012: 243). Teenage drinking and drug abuse may be viewed as delinquency. 2012).

**Demon**: A superhuman being between humans and [gods](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#God/Goddess), which can have benevolent or malevolent intentions based on the religious tradition. In [Christianity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity), they are considered evil. In [Hinduism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Hinduism), demons belong to many castes and are sometimes hard to distinguish from gods (Smith and Green 1995: 311).

Congregations not belonging to a denomination are usually called "independent" or "non-denominational" (Melton 2009: 3).

**Denominational Continuum**: A spectrum of [denominational](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Denomination) characteristics that range from “extremist” religious groups with high demands of sacrifice on one side, and “lenient” groups that demand little of their members on the other side. The “extremist” groups tend to be exclusive, strict, small, and suspicious of others, while the “lenient” groups tend to be inclusive, less costly, larger, and more tolerant of secular values.

**Denominationalism**: Denominationalism refers to the subdivision of a particular religion. A common example is [Protestant Christianity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Protestantism) in the United States, which is subdivided into multiple [denominations](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Denomination) (e.g., Baptist, Methodist, etc.).

**Deuterocanonical Books**: See [Apocrypha](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Apocrypha).

**Devotionalism**: The frequency at which an individual performs [religious rituals](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Rituals,%20Religious) and comparable behaviors, notably prayer and [Bible](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Bible,%20Christian) reading, often measured independently of group activities such as church attendance (Roof 1976).

**Dharma**: The proper course of conduct, norms and ultimate realities in the [Buddhist](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Buddhism) religion. Dharma is central to Buddhist practice. The term also exists in [Hinduism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Hinduism) and Brahmanic thought as a set of ritual actions sanctioned by the priestly class (Smith and Green 1995: 315).

**Dialectical Imagination**: A religious perspective emphasizing the individual and the withdrawal of [God](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#God/Goddess) from the [sinful](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sin) world.

**Diaspora**: The dispersion of a religious people outside their geographic homeland, where they must live as a minority among others (Esposito et al. 2012: G-4).

**Diocese**: The wider regional structure connecting [parishes](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Parish) and other local organizations that is overseen by a [bishop](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Bishop) (Reid et al. 1990: 357).

**Disaffiliation**: The opposite of [conversion](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Conversion), disaffiliation refers to the process of leaving a religious organization or disavowing one's former [religious identity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religious%20Identity).

**Disciple**: A pupil who is attached to a specific teacher or way of life (Smith and Green 1995: 317). In the [Christian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) tradition, John the Baptist and [Jesus](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ) had disciples. Peter is a famous disciple of Jesus. The term also has been used in the [Buddhist](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Buddhism) tradition. For example, [Ananda](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Ananda) was a disciple and cousin of the [Buddha](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Siddhartha%20Gautama).

**Dispensational Premillennialism**: The belief held by some [Christians](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christians) that the current dispensation, or historical period, is near the end, and will conclude with the [rapture](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Rapture) of the believers into [heaven](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Heaven%20(Christianity)). [Jesus](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ) will come down from heaven to fight the [Antichrist](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Antichrist) and establish a [thousand-year reign of peace](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Premillennialism%20(Chiliasm)). This type of theology was made popular by the [Scofield Reference Bible](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=97) and the fictional [_Left Behind_](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=52) book series.

**Dispensationalism**: A [Christian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) [theological](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Theology) view that divides history into several periods, or dispensations. God's plan for [salvation](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Salvation) differs according to the dispensation (Smith and Green 1995: 318).

**Divination**: The determination of the hidden significance of things through a variety of techniques. Divination often is performed by specialists and is historically common in Chinese and Japanese [religions](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religion) (Smith and Green 1995: 318-319).

**Divinity**: A term frequently used prior to the 20th century to refer to the study of [theology](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Theology) or the "science of divine things." The term also could refer to the quality of being divine as well as to God himself (Reid et al. 1990: 359).

**Doctrine**: An official teaching of a religious group. In a Christian context, the [Trinity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Trinity) serves as an important doctrine. In [Buddhist](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Buddhism), [Hindu](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Hinduism), and [Jainist](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jainism) traditions, [ahimsa](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Ahimsa) is an important doctrine (McBrien 1995: 424).

**Dogma**: Dogma is understood as a principle component of a religious ideology that is non-disputable. The Greek word is "dokeo," which means "appears." Dogma is particularly found in [Roman Catholicism](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=708), explicitly stated in ecumenical councils or by the [pope](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Pope). In the context of the Catholic Church, the [Nicene Creed](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Nicene%20Creed) contains dogmata (Reid et al. 1990: 361; McBrien 1995: 424).

**Dome of the Rock**: A domed shrine in [Jerusalem](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jerusalem) that houses the rock upon which the [Prophet Muhammad](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Muhammad%20(Mohammad)) ascended into the Seven Heavens during his [night journey](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Night%20Journey).

**Dominionism**: The belief that Christians should hold positions of power in society and government based on biblical law. Dominionism has close ties to [Christian nationalism](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive/measurements/single-item-measures?scid=133), which suggests that it is important to reunite church and state in the United States because the Founding Fathers believed in a Christian nation.

**Faith Healing**: A term usually limited to the [Christian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) practice of restoring health by means of [prayer](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Prayer), divine power or the intervention of the [Holy Spirit](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Holy%20Spirit) (Smith and Green 1995: 355).

**Family, Religious**: See [religious family](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religious%20Family).

**Fanatic**: A derogatory term for someone overly zealous in their religious faith (Smith and Green 1995: 356).

**Fasting**: The religious practice of abstaining from food for a certain period of time. There are various forms of fasting in the three Abrahamic religions: [Judaism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Judaism), [Christianity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) and [Islam](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Islam). The Jewish [passover](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Passover) includes a fast, [Lent](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Lent) usually includes a chosen fast for Christians, and [Ramadan](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Ramadan) in [Islam](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Islam) includes a month-long daytime fast (Smith and Green 1995: 357).

**Fatalism**: The belief that all events are predetermined, and human effort is therefore irrelevant (Smith and Green 1995: 357).

**Fatwa**: The legal opinion of a private religious scholar concerning [Islamic law](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sharia).

**Feminist Theology**: A system of religious thought that interprets practices and scriptures through a feminist perspective. This perspective spans across [Christian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity), [Jewish](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Judaism), [Muslim](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Islam), and other religions (Lippy and Williams 2000).

**Free-Rider Problem**: In general, a free-rider problem occurs when individuals take advantage of common resource or common goods without paying for or contributing to them. For example, attending holiday services, but not weekly services, may be seen as a form of “free-riding,” as one is relying on others to maintain the congregation for the remainder of the year. Free-riding is more common in low commitment religious organizations and may explain some of the decline that Mainline Protestant denominations have experienced (Stark and Finke 2000). In contrast, high commitment religious organizations demand such high costs that they may scare away potential “free riders” who would otherwise dilute their religious product (Iannaccone 1992).

## M [▲](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#startofdictionary)
**Madrasa**: The term is most often used to describe [Islamic](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Islam) schools, including Islamic universities, seminaries, primary and secondary schools. The term literally means "a place where learning or studying occurs." While some madrasas teach a radical view of Islam, most historically do not. Critics of Barack Obama have equated madrasas with terrorist training schools in order to malign the president's early schooling (Esposito 2011: 40-41).

**Magic**: A term referring to all efforts to manipulate supernatural forces to gain rewards, or avoid costs, without a reference to a [god or gods](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#God/Goddess) or to general explanations of existence (Stark and Finke 2000: 279).

**Mahayana Buddhism**: A school of [Buddhism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Buddhism) that is much more open to the role of nonmonks in the faith. The school dates itself to [Ananda](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Ananda) and other early [disciples](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Disciple) of [Buddha](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Siddhartha%20Gautama) (Melton 2009: 1043).

While Mainline Protestantism is usually seen as more theologically and socially liberal than Evangelical Protestantism, there is obviously variation between denominations, congregations, and individuals within the "Mainline" category (Reid et al. 1990: 700).

**Marital Instability, Religion and**: Marital instability is ongoing conflict in marriage either because of communication problems, disagreements about parenting or gender roles, financial difficulties, lack of trust, or presence of alcohol or drug problems (Koenig et al. 2012: 256). Lack of marital happiness, infidelity, abuse and divorce represent aspects of marital instability.

**Martyr**: In [Judaism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Judaism), [Christianity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) and [Islam](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Islam), a martyr is someone who dies, typically premature and violently, for a [sacred](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sacred) cause. During the late 20th and early 21st centuries, martyrdom became a terrorist strategy for suicide bombers in Israel, Iraq, the United States, and other countries (Prothero 2008: 248).

Her miraculous [virgin birth](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Virgin%20Birth) is recorded in the [gospels](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Gospels). She is frequently depicted in Eastern [icons](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Icon) and Western art. In the Catholic tradition, she is seen as a powerful mediator between the individual and God. The [Protestant](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Protestantism) Reformers criticized what they believed was an excessive veneration of Mary (Smith and Green 1995: 687).

A [gnostic](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Gnosticism) gospel presents her as one of the most important disciples of Jesus. A later tradition depicted her as a prostitute, which is not evident in the gospels (Smith and Green 1995: 687).
