For more information on the Massachusetts Bay Colony, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=55).

**Matha**: A term for a [Hindu](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Hinduism) monastery; also used in [Jainism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jainism) (Esposito et al. 2012b: G-10).

**Meaning Making**: See [Global Meaning](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Global%20Meaning).

**Mecca**: The most holy city in [Islam](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Islam), located in modern-day Saudi Arabia. It was the birthplace of the [Prophet Muhammad](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Muhammad%20(Mohammad)) and is the location for the [sacred](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sacred) [Kaaba](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Kaaba). When [Muslims](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Muslim) go on their [pilgrimage](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Hajj%20(Pilgrimage)) (hajj), they visit Mecca. Muslims pray toward this city as well (Esposito 2011: 245).

**Medina**: The second most holy city in [Islam](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Islam) after [Mecca](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Mecca). It is located in modern day Saudi Arabia. [Muslims](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Muslim) view the city as holy because [Muhammad](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Muhammad%20(Mohammad)) fled to Medina in 622 CE (see [Hijra](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Hijra)) and established the [Muslim community](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Ummah) there before returning to Mecca. In Medina, Muhammad established himself as a politician and military leader in addition to being a religious leader (Prothero 2008: 251).

**Meditation**: A process of serious contemplation that is common in Eastern religions. In [Buddhism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Buddhism), it refers to a range of conscious-altering practices used to remove passion and ignorance, leading to [nirvana](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Nirvana).

**Megachurch**: A large [congregation](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Congregation) with 2,000 or more people attending services. It is typically [Protestant](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Protestantism), often [evangelical](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Evangelical%20Protestantism). Two-thirds of megachurches are affiliated with a [denomination](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Denomination). Currently, there are more than 1,200 megachurches in the United States. Famous megachurch [pastors](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Pastor) include Joel Osteen and Rick Warren (Prothero 2008: 251).

**Member**: 1) A member is a person belonging to a [congregation](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Congregation) and/or [denomination](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Denomination). For example, there may be confessions, behaviors, [rituals](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Rituals,%20Religious) or other requirements for becoming a full member. 2) Sometimes people use the word "member" to mean that they simply attend a congregation, whether they are full members of the congregation or denomination. In this sense, "member" is similar to [adherent](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Adherent).

**Menorah**: A seven-branched candle stand first mentioned in the Book of Exodus. It is a strong symbol of [Jewish](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Judaism) identity, and is associated with modern [Israel](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Israel) (Smith and Green 1995: 700).

**Mental Health**: Mental health broadly refers to a person's psychological and emotional condition.

**Mental Health Measures**: Questions covering issues pertaining to an individual’s [mental health](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Mental%20Health), views of mental health, attitudes toward those with mental health issues, medication, government intervention, etc. [HEALTH2](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?tab=2&fid=MIROLA97#HEALTH2) - 1997 Faith and Community Survey of Four Indianapolis Neighborhoods, [MNTLHLTH](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?tab=2&fid=GSS2004#MNTLHLTH) - 2004 General Social Survey, [EVMHP](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?tab=2&fid=GSS1996#EVMHP) - 1996 General Social Survey, [OUTSIDER](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?tab=2&fid=GSS2002#OUTSIDER) - 2002 General Social Survey, [PSYCMED4](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?tab=2&fid=GSS2006#PSYCMED4) - 2006 General Social Survey, [SEENMNTL](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?tab=2&fid=GSS1998#SEENMNTL) - 1998 General Social Survey [SPMENTL](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?tab=2&fid=GSS2002#MNTLHLTH%3EMNTLHLTH%3C/a%3E%20-%202002%20General%20Social%20Survey,%20%20%3Ca%20href=) - 1996 General Social Survey, [KNWMHOSP](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?tab=2&fid=GSS1996#KNWMHOSP) - 1996 General Social Survey, [MHTRTSLF](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?tab=2&fid=GSS2006#MHTRTSL) - 2006 General Social Survey.

**Mental Health, Religion and**: [Mental health](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Mental%20Health) consists of positive and negative dimensions. Positive mental health includes positive emotions (e.g., happiness, peace, etc.) as well as positive cognitive processes (e.g., optimistic thinking and adaptation), while negative mental health involves emotions, cognitions and behaviors that cause dysfunction in social relationships, occupation and recreation, and interfere with adaptation (e.g., anger, violence, addiction, etc.; see Koenig et al. 2012: 298). For example, traditional religiousness is associated with the negative personality traits of [authoritarianism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Authoritarianism) (Shaffer and Hastings 2007; Watson et al. 2003) and neuroticism (Duriez and Soenens 2006; Jaarmsa et al. 2007).

For instance, the creation of the [Evangelical Lutheran Church in America](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=314) in 1988 was the result of a merger of three smaller [Lutheran](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=90) denominations. Denominations with low tension will typically have declining membership, and are therefore more likely to form mergers (Stark and Finke 2000: 206). See the [Denominations](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups) section to explore denominational histories, including mergers.

**[Merton, Thomas (1915-1968)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=70)**: Thomas Merton was a [Catholic](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Catholicism,%20Roman) [monk](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Monk) and prolific writer. For more information on Thomas Merton, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=70).

**Messiah**: The long-awaited king who will come in the last days. In the [Jewish](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Judaism) tradition, the messiah will restore the Jews to the promised land, rebuild the temple, and inaugurate a period of peace. This is particularly emphasized in [Orthodox Judaism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Orthodox%20Judaism). In the [Christian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) tradition, [Jesus](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ) is the messiah, but most Jews do not hold this view, with the exception of [Jews for Jesus](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jews%20for%20Jesus) and some messianic Jewish groups (Prothero 2008: 252).

**Methodist-Pietist Family**: The [Methodist-Pietist](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=92) family consists of [churches](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Church) that stress the importance of internal faith, spirituality and Christian living over adherence to formal [creeds](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Creed) and doctrine. The largest among these churches is the [United Methodist Church](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=854), which follows the teachings of [John Wesley](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Wesley,%20John%20(1703-1791)), who in the 18th century broke away from the Church of England because of his emphasis on personal holiness. Methodism came to the United States in the 1760s with Leesburg, Virginia being the site of the first Methodist society (Melton 2009: 273-274).

In understanding the impact of migration on religion, the migration of Catholic immigrants in the 19th and early 20th century allowed [Catholicism](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=87) to go from a small firm to one with a quarter of consumers (Finke and Stark 1992).

**Millenarianism**: The belief that there will be an unprecedented period of peace and righteousness on the earth, usually associated with the [return of Jesus Christ](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Second%20Coming). Millennial groups are typically divided into [premillennialist](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Premillennialism%20(Chiliasm)) and [postmillennialist](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Postmillennialism) perspectives based on beliefs regarding the return of Christ and the events preceding his return. [Amillennialism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Amillennialism) is sometimes considered a third perspective, although it mostly deals with a symbolic interpretation of the "millenium" (Smith and Green 1995: 738).

**[Miller, William (1782-1849)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=116)**: William Miller was a [Baptist](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Baptist) lay preacher who predicted that the return of Christ would occur in 1843. Despite his failed predictions, his teachings influenced both [Ellen Gould White](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=117) and her husband, [James Springer White](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=118). They would later found the [Seventh-day Adventist Church](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=743). For more information on William Miller, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=116).

**[Million Man March](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=114)**: The Million Man March of 1995, organized by the [Nation of Islam's](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Nation%20of%20Islam) Louis Farrakhan, was the largest gathering of African Americans in U.S. history. For more information on the Million Man March, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=114).

**Minister**: 1) One who performs a number of [church](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Church) duties. 2) The title for a preacher or [pastor](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Pastor) in many [Protestant](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Protestantism) churches (Smith and Green 1995: 721).

**Miracle**: The dwelling place of God, [angels](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Angel) and redeemed individuals in the [afterlife](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Afterlife). It functions as the ultimate reward for the redeemed, as opposed to [hell](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Hell%20(Christianity)), which is the punishment for the [damned](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Damnation) (Smith and Green 1995: 411).

**[Mitt Romney's 2012 Presidential Campaign](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=146)**: Mitt Romney became the first [Mormon](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Mormon) nominee for president when he ran as a Republican in 2012 against Barack Obama. For more on Mitt Romney and his religious faith, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=146).

**Moksha**: A [Hindu](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Hinduism) concept meaning the release of [samsara](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Samsara), or the life cycle from birth, life, death and rebirth. In [Buddhism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Buddhism), this concept is known as [nirvana](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Nirvana) (Esposito et al. 2012a: G-4).

**Monasticism**: A form of religious organization that emphasizes strict [ascetic](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Asceticism) practices and individual [salvation](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Salvation). Monasticism was fairly dominant in the medieval ages. It has waned since the [Protestant](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Protestantism) Reformation, but still exists in Catholic and [Orthodox](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=89) traditions. Monasticism also is fairly prominent in the [Buddhist](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Buddhism) tradition (Smith and Green 1995: 727).

**Monk**: Male member of a monastic community (Smith and Green 1995: 728). See [Monasticism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Monasticism).

**Mono/Multi-Racial Group**: This refers to the amount of racial and/or ethnic diversity within a [religious group](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religious%20Group).

**Monotheism**: The belief that there is only one God, shared by [Jews](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Judaism), [Christians](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christians) and [Muslims](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Muslim). This is in contrast to [polytheism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Polytheism), which posits multiple gods, and [atheism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Atheism), which posits that there is no God (Prothero 2008: 253).

**Monstrance**: A vessel, typically made of metal, used to display the [Eucharistic](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Eucharist) bread in [Catholic](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Catholicism,%20Roman) and [Anglican](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Anglican%20Family) churches. It is also known as an ostensorium (McBrien 1995:890).

**[Moody, Dwight (1837-1899)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=37)**: Dwight L. Moody was a 19th century [Protestant](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Protestantism) [revivalist](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Revivalist) whose popularity led to the Moody Bible Institute and the growth of [Christian fundamentalism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Fundamentalism). For more information on Dwight Moody, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=37).

**Moonie**: A popular name for [members](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Member) of the controversial Unification Church (Smith and Green 1995: 728). See [Unification Church](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Unification%20Church).

**[Moral Majority](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=46)**: A conservative political group seeking to "return" Judeo-Christian morality to society. For more information, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=46).

**Mormon**: A member who belongs to a [church](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Church) in the Latter-day Saint Family. See [Latter-day Saints Family](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=100) for more.

**Moroni**: The last of the Nephite [prophets](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Prophet) who resurrected in the form of an [angel](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Angel) to reveal to [Joseph Smith](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=43) where he buried sacred golden plates 14 centuries earlier. This occurred on September 21, 1823 (Smith and Green 1995: 731).

**Moses**: A very important [prophet](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Prophet) in [Judaism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Judaism), [Christianity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity), and [Islam](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Islam). He is remembered for leading the Jewish slaves out of Egypt and receiving the [Ten Commandments](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Ten%20Commandments%20(Decalogue)) from God on Mount Sinai. The revelations on Mount Sinai became known as the [Torah](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Torah), or Law.

**Mosque**: The [Islamic](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Islam) building for public worship. The term "mosque" comes from the Arabic word "masjid," meaning "place for ritual prostration." The first mosque was founded by the [Prophet Muhammad](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Muhammad%20(Mohammad)) in Medina as a place for worship and [prayer](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Prayer). There are more than 2,100 mosques located in the United States (Esposito 2011: 38-39).

**Muhammad (Mohammad)**: The founder and last [prophet](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Prophet) in [Islam](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Islam). He was born in [Mecca](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Mecca) (570 CE) and died in [Medina](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Medina) (632 CE). He was born an orphan and became a trader. He received his first of many revelations at age 40 from the [angel](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Angel) [Gabriel](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Gabriel) in a cave. These revelations covered issues of God's nature, morality, other prophets (including [Jesus](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ)) and more. His followers recorded his accounts, which later became the [Koran](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Koran). After his enemies attempted to kill him, he fled to Medina in 622 C.E., where he established his Muslim community. He returned to Mecca with his army in 630 C.E., and demolished the [idols](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Idol) around the [Kaaba](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Kaaba). In Islam, the phrase "peace be upon him" follows any utterance of his name (Prothero 2008: 257-258).

**Muslim**: An [adherent](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Adherent) of Islam. See [Islam](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Islam).

**Mystical Experience**: Some sense of contact, however fleeting, with a [god or gods](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#God/Goddess).

**Mysticism**: A form of spirituality stressing union with God and religious experience, rather than doctrine. Mystical traditions transcend religious traditions, evident in the three major world religions of [Christianity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity), [Islam](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Islam), and [Judaism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Judaism) (Smith and Green 1995: 747-748).

**Mythological Religion**: A reinterpretation of religious statements to seek their deeper symbolic meanings (Hunt 1972).

## N [▲](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#startofdictionary)
**Nation of Islam**: An American movement founded in the [early 20th century](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=112) that emphasizes that [Islam](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Islam) is the true religion of black people and that African-Americans should leave the distorted white [religion](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religion) of [Christianity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity). The movement spread throughout the country under Elijah Muhammad and became increasingly militant after World War II (Mead et al. 2005: 379-380).

**National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health)**: The National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health) is a nationally representative study that follows a sample of adolescents (Wave 1: 1994-1995) as they grow into adults.

**Native American Church**: A movement among Native Americans that has factions related to [Christianity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity), but diverges from popular aspects of Christianity through the use of cactus peyote for ceremonial purposes. Their use of peyote is legal in the United States since it is being used for "religious" purposes (Esposito et al. 2012b: 64).

**Naturalistic Determinism**: The notion that all things can be understood in terms of natural scientific principles and laws. Popular in the late 19th and early 20th century, this belief allowed scholars like J.H. Leuba, Emile Durkheim, E.D. Starbuck and William James to begin studying religion scientifically (Koenig et al. 2012: 31).

**Near-Death Experience (NDE)**: The concept of near-death experiences (NDEs) became popular in the 1970s, as some have claimed to die, experience the afterlife and return to life telling others about their experience. In any case, NDEs continue to be popular among the highly religious, as evidenced by _New York Times_ best-selling 2010 book _Heaven is for Real_.

**Neo-Confucianism**: A tradition that attempts to harmonize the spiritual teachings of [Confucius](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Confucianism) with the cosmology of [Taoism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Taoism) and the teaching of [karma](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Karma) in [Buddhism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Buddhism). It also incorporates [meditation](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Meditation) techniques from both Taoism and Buddhism (Esposito et al. 2012b: G-16).

**Neopaganism**: A diverse, decentralized religious movement that emphasizes the importance of nature, [polytheism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Polytheism), [pantheism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Pantheism), personal responsibility and [rituals](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Rituals,%20Religious). Neopagan religions include reconstructions of Egyptian, Celtic, Norse and Greek Paganism as well as Neopagan Witchcraft ( [Wicca](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Wicca)). The movement has more than 100,000 [adherents](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Adherent) in the United States and Canada (Smith and Green 1995: 765).

**New Age**: A loosely based movement that emerged in the late 1960s stressing experiential spirituality, the interconnectedness of life and the immanence (or nearness) of the [sacred](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sacred) to the world, drawing on a blend of [occult](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Occultism), Eastern and human potential teachings. [Evangelical](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Evangelical%20Protestantism) churches in the United States and Europe have denounced New Age movements as detrimental to Christian values (Smith and Green 1995: 768-769).

**New Religious Movements**: Groups and movements that because of belief and practice exist outside of traditional [Christianity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity), [Judaism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Judaism), and other major religious traditions. Examples of new religious movements would be the [Unification Church](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Unification%20Church) and various [neopagan](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Neopaganism) groups, although even such an established religion as Christianity started out as a new religious movement within Judaism. Scholars prefer the term "New Religious Movement" over ["cult"](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Cult) because the term "cult" is more of a political term used to denounce new religious groups. There is little evidence that new religious movements actually use "brainwashing" (Stark and Finke 2000: 136).

**New Testament**: Canonized [scripture](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Scriptures) in addition to the [Old Testament](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Old%20Testament%20(Hebrew%20Bible)) that constitutes the [Christian Bible](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Bible,%20Christian). The first four books are the [gospels](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Gospels), which record the life of [Jesus Christ](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ). Among the gospels, the first three (Matthew, Mark, and Luke) are considered the synoptic gospels for their similarity in content, whereas the book of John is considered fairly distinct. Most of the New Testament contains letters, many of whom are attributed to the [apostle](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Apostle) Paul, while others are either anonymous or associated with other early church leaders. The New Testament ends with the book of Revelation, an [apocalypse](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Apocalypse) that deals with the [end-times](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#End-Times) as well as with current persecution at the hands of the Romans. The New Testament was officially [canonized](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Canon) in 367 by Bishop Athanasius of Alexandria (Smith and Green 1995: 769-770).

**Nicene Creed**: A formal [creed](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Creed) stating that [Jesus](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ) was "the only-begotten Son of God, begotten of the Father before all worlds, God of God, Light of Light, Very God of Very God." Most [Catholics](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=87), [Protestants](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Protestantism), and [Orthodox](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=89) Christians affirm this creed (Prothero 2008: 239).

**[Niebuhr, Reinhold (1892-1971)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=50)**: Reinhold Niebuhr (1892-1971) was an influential [Christian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) [theologian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Theologian) in the 20th century. He also is credited with the popular Serenity Prayer. For more information on Reinhold Niebuhr, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=50).

**Night Journey**: The Prophet [Muhammad's](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Muhammad%20(Mohammad)) journey from [Mecca](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Mecca) to [Jerusalem](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jerusalem), and then from Jerusalem into heaven where he met [Abraham](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Abraham), [Moses](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Moses), [Jesus](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ), and other [prophets](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Prophet). This event is briefly discussed in the [Koran](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Koran) and further elaborated in the [hadith](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Hadith). The Night Journey made Jerusalem the third-holiest city, behind Mecca and [Medina](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Medina), in [Islam](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Islam). It also affirmed the continuity of Islam with [Judaism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Judaism) and [Christianity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) (Esposito 2011: 188).

**Nirvana**: The main religious goal in major forms of [Hinduism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Hinduism) and [Buddhism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Buddhism). The term comes from Sanskrit, meaning "blowing out." It is essentially the extinction of suffering and the liberation from [samsara](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Samsara). It is important to note that [Mahayana Buddhists](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Mahayana%20Buddhism) do not see a clear distinction between nirvana and samsara, seeing the world of suffering as nirvana itself (Prothero 2008: 259).

**Nominal Christian**: A term for those who identify as [Christian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christians) in name only, meaning that they aren't particularly religious. This identification is contrasted with practicing Christians, and is often used in a pejorative way (Reid et al. 1990: 827).

**Numinous**: A primary sense of religious experience, an overwhelming feeling of the divine. The German [theologian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Theologian) Rudolf Otto coined this term in his 1917 book _The Idea of the Holy_ (Smith and Green 1995: 804).

**Nun**: A term referring to any [Catholic](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=708), [Orthodox](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=89) or [Anglican](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=88) woman who is an avowed member of the religious community. Technically, it refers to women who take a solemn oath to renounce a life of pleasure and live a life of [prayer](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Prayer) and discipline in a monastery (Reid et al. 1990: 832).

## P [▲](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#startofdictionary)
**Pali Canon**: The complete [canon](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Canon) among the early collections of the [Buddha's](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Siddhartha%20Gautama) teachings. The [canon](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Canon) is split into three sections: _Vinaya_ (monastic code), _Sutras_ (sermons), and _Abhidhamma_ (advanced teaching formula) (Esposito et al. 2012b: G-13).

**Palm Sunday**: The first day of [Holy Week](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Holy%20Week) that commemorates [Jesus'](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ) triumphant entry into [Jerusalem](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jerusalem). It is celebrated a week before [Easter](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Easter) (Smith and Green 1995: 827).

**Pantheism**: The belief that all of reality is divine. It can be cosmic in the sense that God is equated with nature, or acosmic in the sense that experience is illusory and only the divine is real (Hinnells 1984: 245).

**Papal Infallibility**: A [Roman Catholic](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=708) term referring to the [pope's](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Pope) share in the general [grace](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Grace) that preserves the Church from error. This term was formally defined by the Roman Catholic Church in 1870 at the [First Vatican Council](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Vatican%20Council%20I) (Reid et al. 1990: 862).

**Paranormal, Measures of**: [Survey](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Survey) questions aimed at gauging an individual’s belief in and experience of the “paranormal.” Ghosts and unidentified monsters are potential topics that are covered.

Examples of this [measure](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Measure/Measurement) are found in the [2005 Baylor Religion Survey](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?fid=BRS2005), [2003 National Study of Youth and Religion](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?fid=NSYRW1) and [1998 General Social Survey](https://www.thearda.com/data-archive?fid=GSS1998), all of which are available in the ARDA’s Data Archive.

**Parish**: Another name for a [congregation](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Congregation) found predominantly in [Roman Catholic](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=708), [Orthodox](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=89) and [Anglican](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=88) churches (Smith and Green 1995: 829).

**Parochial Schools**: [Parish-supported](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Parish) [Catholic](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=87), usually elementary, schools (Reid et al. 1990: 868).

**Particularism**: This refers to the belief that only one's own faith is true or that [salvation](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Salvation) can be achieved only by adherence to a particular [religion](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religion).

**Passover**: A seven-day [Jewish](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Judaism) holiday commemorating the story in Exodus where God saved the Jewish people from slavery in Egypt. No leavened bread is eaten during this holiday, and matzah is considered the staple food (Hinnells 1991: 35).

**Pastor**: [Ordained](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Ordination) leader of a [congregation](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Congregation). In [Catholicism](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=87), the term can also mean the head [priest](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Priest) of a [parish](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Parish) (Reid et al. 1990: 871).

**Patriarch**: 1) The head [bishop](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Bishop) of an [Eastern Orthodox Church](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=89) (see [Athenagoras I of Constantinople, 1886-1972](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=141)). 2) A historical title for the bishops in the ancient cities of Rome, Alexandria, Antioch, Constantinople, and Jerusalem. 3) A term for [Abraham](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Abraham), Isaac, and Jacob in the [Hebrew Bible](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Bible,%20Hebrew%20(Tanakh)) (Smith and Green 1995: 833).

**Patriarchate**: A seat of authority in the [Eastern Orthodox churches](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=89). See [Patriarch](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Patriarch).

**Paul**: A first-century [church](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Church) leader in [Christianity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) and the author of many [New Testament](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#New%20Testament) epistles. He was born [Jewish](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jews) and was called Saul, a Pharisee and persecutor of [Christians](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christians). According to the Book of Acts, he saw the [resurrected](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Resurrection) [Christ](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ) on the road to Damascus and [converted](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Conversion) to Christianity. Afterward, he preached the gospel to Jews and Christians alike.

**[Penn, William (1644-1718)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=125)**: William Penn was a [Quaker](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=95) activist, [religious tolerance](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religious%20Tolerance) advocate, and founder of the Pennsylvania colony. He wrote many books on his religious faith and the ideal style of government, including _No Cross, No Crown_ (1669) and _Frame of Government_ (1682), the latter of which influenced the U.S. Constitution. For more information on William Penn, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=125).

**Pentecost**: The annual [Christian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) celebration commemorating the descent of the [Holy Spirit](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Holy%20Spirit) on the [disciples](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Disciple) of [Jesus](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ) as recorded in the biblical book of Acts. The term derives from Greek, literally meaning "50 days," traditionally the time between the [Passover](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Passover) feast and the wheat harvest. In the early church and in some churches today, Pentecost is celebrated fifty days following [Easter](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Easter). Later [Judaism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Judaism) associated Pentecost with God giving [Moses](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Moses) the [Law](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Torah) on Mount Sinai. The Christian celebration is common in [liturgical](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Liturgy) churches with the final lighting of the Paschal candle, readings from the lectionary, and [prayer](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Prayer) (Reid et al. 1990: 881).

**[Pentecostal Family](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=94)**: A movement of [churches](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Church) that [emerged in early 20th century America](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=211), stressing enthusiastic worship and the restoration of such practices evident in [New Testament](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#New%20Testament) [Christianity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity), such as [speaking in tongues](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Speaking%20In%20Tongues) and [healing](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Faith%20Healing). It is sometimes divided into "classical Pentecostalism," indicating the movement's historical bodies, and "neo-Pentecostalism," the modern movement emphasizing [charismatic](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Charismatics) renewal (Reid et al. 1990: 885-886).

**People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab)**: In [Islam](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Islam), this refers to non-Muslims who possess some revelation or [scripture](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Scriptures) from God. [Jews](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jews) and [Christians](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christians) make up this group, and sometimes [Zoroastrians](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Zoroastrians) are included (Esposito et al. 2012b: G-9).

**People's Temple**: A controversial [new religious movement](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#New%20Religious%20Movements) that was founded by [Jim Jones](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jones,%20Jim) in the 1960s. The [congregation](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Congregation) was known for its racial diversity, emphasizing anti-racial themes along with socialist ideals. Jones became increasingly paranoid about government authorities, moving followers from California to Guyana, where he established an isolated farming community dubbed Jonestown. The group would routinely practice mass suicide rituals. Thereafter, Jones gave members poisoned fruit punch in a mass suicide, often argued as murder. Jones and more than 900 members died on November 18, 1978 (Smith and Green 1995: 836).

For instance, if you take the total amount of money received by a congregation and divided by the number of [members](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Member), you would have "giving per capita," or the average amount of money given per person.

**Personality Disorders, Religion and**: A personality disorder is an extreme expression of personality traits. Many personality disorders feature high neuroticism and low extraversion, leading to emotional distress and social withdrawal. Schizophrenia, borderline personality disorder, narcissism, antisocial disorder and obsessive compulsiveness are all considered personality disorders. Although studies on religion and personality disorders are not abundant, research has found that religiousness is less common among paranoid schizophrenics (Joseph and Diduca 2001), those with borderline (Maltby et al. 2000), narcissistic (Sandage et al. 2000) and antisocial personality traits (Kerley, Matthews and Blanchard 2005). Moreover, religiousness is more common among those with obsessive-compulsive personality traits (see Flannelly et al. 2006).

**Personality, Religion and**: Personality is a person’s unique characteristic way of thinking, feeling and behaving; a set of psychological characteristics that are relatively stable across different environments and time periods (Koenig et al. 2012: 272). Reviewing studies on personality, Koenig and colleagues (2012) have found that religion tends to be negatively associated with psychoticism (risk taking/lack of responsibility), positively associated with conscientiousness and agreeableness, negatively associated with hostility, and positively associated with [guilt-proneness](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Guilt-oriented,%20Intropunitive%20Religion) as well as [authoritarianism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Authoritarianism).

**Physical Health, Religion and**: Physical health is broad category of health pertaining to the physical body. In the area of religion/spirituality, studies have found that religiousness/spirituality is inversely related to cardiac problems (Chen and Contrada 2007; Contrada et al. 2004), high blood pressure/hypertension (Al-Kandari 2003; Gillum and Ingram 2006), cancer (Oman et al. 2002), while religiousness was positively related to immune functioning (Lutgendorf et al. 2004) and endocrine functioning (Ironson et al. 2002). 2012). Positive coping, beneficial health practices and support from religious communities may all play a role in explaining the results (see [Coping Theory](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Coping%20Theory); [Health Behaviors, Religion and](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Health%20Behaviors,%20Religion%20and)).

**Pluralism**: The existence or toleration of diverse religious groups in a society. For example, America is a religiously pluralistic country because it has many different [denominations](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Denomination) and [religions](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religion).

**[Plymouth Plantation](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=54)**: Plymouth Plantation was a North American colony settled in 1620 by English Separatists, later known as Pilgrims, who desired to practice their own religion freely. For more information on Plymouth Plantation, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=54).

**Political Islam**: See [Islamism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Islamism).

**Political Opportunity**: Political opportunity theory suggests that changes in the political opportunity structure are a major factor in determining which social movements are viable and successful.

**Polytheism**: The belief in many gods (Prothero 2008: 264).

**Pope**: The appointed leader of the [Roman Catholic Church](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=708) (Smith and Green 1995: 849).

**[Pope John XXIII (1881-1963)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=158)**: [Pope](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Pope) John XXIII called the [Second Vatican Council](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=266), one of the most significant events in the modern [Catholic Church](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Catholicism,%20Roman). Pope John XXIII was canonized a [saint](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Saint) in 2014. For more information on Pope John XXIII, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=158).

**[Pope Paul VI (1897-1978)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=156)**: Pope Paul VI oversaw the completion of the [Second Vatican Council](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=266) and authored [Humanae Vitae](http://w2.vatican.va/content/paul-vi/en/encyclicals/documents/hf_p-vi_enc_25071968_humanae-vitae.html), an important, albeit controversial, document in modern Catholicism that denounced contraception. For more on Pope Paul VI, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=156).

**Postmillennialism**: The belief that the return of [Christ](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ) will take place after the millennium, which may be a literal period of peace and prosperity or else a symbolic representation of the final triumph of the gospel. This view is often dismissed by critics as a Christian version of the [secular](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Secular) idea of progress, but it was actually formulated by Puritan [theologians](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Theologian) (Reid et al. 1990: 919).

**Prayer**: Communication addressed to [god or gods](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#God/Goddess), and sometimes intermediaries. Prayers build confidence and affection between humans and a god or gods (Stark and Finke 2000: 280).

**Prayer, Health Benefits of**: Studies on the health benefits of [prayer](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Prayer) tend to be mixed, particularly in the context of intercessory prayer (praying on the behalf of others). 2012). In sum, the person doing the praying, and how prayer is used in conjunction with medical services, matter when examining the health benefits of prayer.

**Preacher**: A person, traditionally, ordained, who preaches [sermons](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sermon) to a [congregation](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Congregation). It's a common term for [ministers](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Minister) in non- [liturgical](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Liturgy) religious groups.

**Predestination**: The belief that every human being, before birth, was predestined by God to either [heaven](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Heaven%20(Christianity)) or [hell](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Hell%20(Christianity)). This is found in [Calvinist](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Calvinism) [theology](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Theology), also known as Reformed theology (Prothero 2008: 207).

**Premillennialism (Chiliasm)**: The belief that at the end of the present age [Christ](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ) will come back and reign on earth for one thousand years, based on passages in Isaiah 55-66 and Revelation 20:1-10. Before the advent of God's kingdom, premillennialists believe that there will be signs including preaching to all nations, earthquakes, famine, wars, a great [apostasy](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Apostasy), the [Antichrist](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Antichrist), and a period of great tribulation (Reid et al. 1990: 929).

**[Presbyterian-Reformed Family](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=91)**: The [Protestant](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Protestantism) tradition based on the teachings of reformer John Calvin. American Presbyterianism split over revivalism, slavery and fundamentalism, but is still one of the leading Protestant families in the United States (Prothero 2008: 265).

**Presbytery**: An administrative body in a [Presbyterian](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=91) church (Reid et al. 1990: 933).

**Priest**: An [ordained](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Ordination) person who performs religious duties in the [Anglican](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=88), [Catholic](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=87), and [Orthodox](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=89) churches, as well as in world religions such as [Hinduism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Hinduism) (Smith and Green 1995: 858-859).

**Primary Religious Behavior**: “An authentic inner experience of the divine combined with whatever efforts the individual may make to harmonize his/her life with the divine” (Clark 1958:23). This is in contrast to uninspired, or routine religious behavior ( [Secondary Religious Behavior](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Secondary%20Religious%20Behavior)), as well as religious routines accepted on the authority of someone else ( [Tertiary Religious Behavior](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Tertiary%20Religious%20Behavior)).

**Prophecy**: A mode of communication between the divine and specific humans, known as [prophets](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Prophet). In various religious traditions, prophecy often occurs at times of crises, like an imminent military threat or natural disaster (Smith and Green 1995: 861-862).

**Prophet**: The intermediary between the divine and the human audience, communicating with [god/gods](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#God/Goddess) on behalf of other humans. Famous prophets in the Judeo-Christian-Islam traditions include [Abraham](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Abraham), [Moses](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Moses) and the Prophet [Muhammad](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Muhammad%20(Mohammad)). Some other traditions, especially native religions, refer to this type of intermediary as a [shaman](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Shaman), conjurer, spirit or medium (Smith and Green 1995: 861).

**Proselytism**: The practice of seeking to convert people from other [religions](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religion) or no religion to another faith (Melton 2009: 3).

**Prosperity Gospel**: See [Gospel of Wealth](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Gospel%20of%20Wealth).

**Protestant Buddhism**: A term coined by anthropologist Gananath Obeyesekere to describe the adoption of aspects of [missionary](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Mission/Missionary%20Movements) [Protestant Christianity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Protestantism) into [Buddhism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Buddhism) to reinvigorate practices and doctrines. Henry Steele Olcott (1832-1907) was an American convert who went to colonial Sri Lanka, and encouraged Buddhist leaders to emphasize the importance of the [laity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Laity) and reestablish "true Buddhism" (Esposito et al. 2012: 450).

**Protestant Ethic**: Based on Max Weber's ([1904-05] 1996) classic argument about [religion](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religion) and capitalism, this concept brings together supposed characteristics of [Protestantism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Protestantism), such as worldly [asceticism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Asceticism), dedication to work, and the notion that economic success is evidence of [grace](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Grace).

**Protestantism**: A branch of [Christianity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) dating back to the Reformation of the 15th century, when Reformers, such as [Martin Luther](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Luther,%20Martin%20(1483-1546)) and John Calvin, first sought to reform the [Catholic Church](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=708) but increasingly left to start their own [churches](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Church). Most Protestant churches share a belief in the priesthood of all believers, whereas Catholic Churches have a hierarchal model that clearly separates the priesthood [(clergy)](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Clergy) from the members [(laity)](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Laity). Also, Protestants emphasize the sole authority of the [Bible](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Bible,%20Christian) [(sola scriptura)](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sola%20Scriptura), whereas Catholics see church tradition along with the Bible as authorities for faith and practice (Reid et al. 1990: 949).

**Pseudepigrapha**: A collection of [Jewish](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Judaism) and [Christian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity) books written from the third century BCE to the sixth century CE. The term "pseudepigrapha" literally means "writings with false attributions," for they are not regarded as authentic, and therefore not authoritative. However, some parts of the pseudepigrapha are included in the Ethiopian Christian Old Testament (Smith and Green 1995: 55).

**Psychology of Religion**: According to Hood and colleagues (2009), the psychology of religion seeks to comprehend the many ways in which a person’s faith operates in his or her particular world.

**Punya**: Good [karma](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Karma), or merit, in [Buddhism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Buddhism). One accumulates punya through moral actions, learning, and [meditation](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Meditation) (Esposito et al. 2012b: G-14).

**Purgatory**: The place, state or condition of departed [Christian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christians) souls in which they undergo purifying suffering before entering [heaven](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Heaven%20(Christianity)). This belief is evident in [Roman Catholicism](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=708) (Reid et al. 1990: 964).

**Purim**: A [Jewish](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Judaism) holiday commemorating the events in the book of Esther, where Queen Esther saved the [Jews](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jews) of the Persian Empire from the designs of the villainous Haman. Some Jews wear costumes on this day and send food to one another (Hinnells 1991: 35).

## W [▲](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#startofdictionary)\
  
**Wahhabism**: A conservative [Sunni Muslim](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sunni%20Islam) movement that seeks to return the Muslim world to the pure [Islam](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Islam) in the [Koran](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Koran) and restore traditional morality in society. The term derives from the founder of the movement, Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab (1703-1792), although the term is considered derogatory. Proponents of the movement prefer being called "Muwahhidun" or Salafis. It recently spread to Afghanistan through the [Taliban](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Taliban), and has influenced leaders of [al-Qaeda](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Al-Qaeda), like Osama bin Laden (Prothero 2008: 290).   
  
**Ward**: A [congregation](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Congregation) in the [Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (Mormon)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=100).   
  
**Warrior Monks**: Japanese [Buddhist](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Buddhism) [monks](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Monk) who participated in armed violence in the eighth century. Warrior monks were particularly influential in eleventh through twelfth centuries, but their influence abated when Japan was unified in the sixteenth century (Smith and Green 1995: 1130).   
  
**[Wesley, Charles (1707-1788)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=76)**: Charles Wesley was an important leader of the [Methodist](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Methodist-Pietist%20Family) movement. He was influential in having his brother, [John](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=75), join the group that eventually became the Methodists. He also was a prolific hymn writer. Some of his well-known hymns include "Hark! The Herald Angels Sing" and "Christ the Lord Is Risen Today." For more information on Charles Wesley, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=76).   
  
**Wesley, John (1703-1791)**: The founder of [Methodism](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=92). He was [ordained](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Ordination) in 1725 in the Church of England. From 1729 to 1735, he led the Holy Club, a group of students who were called Methodists. They performed acts of piety and charity. After his disastrous [missionary](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Mission/Missionary%20Movements) trip to America, he returned to England. In 1738, he had a [religious experience](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religious%20Experience) that convinced him the activities of the Methodists could be empowered by [grace](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Grace) through faith in [Jesus](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ). 1990: 1241). For more information on John Wesley, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=75).  
  
**[Western Liturgical Family](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=87)**: [Churches](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Church) represented by or originating from the [Roman Catholic Church](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=708). Such offshoots include the Old Catholic Church and the Polish National Catholic Church, which differ from the Roman Catholic Church in their rejection of the authority of the [pope](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Pope) (Melton 2009: 82). To interactively explore the history of Catholics in America, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/interactive-display?tid=7).   
  
**Westminster Abbey**: The central church of English [Christianity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity).   
  
**[White, Ellen Gould (1827-1915)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=117)**: Ellen Gould White was the co-founder of the [Seventh-day Adventist Church](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=743), along with her husband, [James Springer White](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=118). She promoted Saturday as the Christian [Sabbath](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sabbath) and advocated biblically-based health initiatives. For more information on Ellen White, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=117).   
  
**[White, James Springer (1821-1881)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=118)**: James Springer White was the co-founder of the [Seventh-day Adventist Church](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=743), along with his wife [Ellen Gould White](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=117). For more information on James Springer White, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=118).   
  
**[Whitefield, George (1714-1770)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=94)**: George Whitefield was the leading [preacher](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Preacher) and [revivalist](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Revivalist) of the [First Great Awakening](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=324) in the American colonies. George Whitefield was a Church of England clergyman and itinerant preacher who made seven trips to the American colonies, attracting large crowds during this ["preaching tours."](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=1&eid=230) For more information on George Whitefield, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=94).   
  
**Wicca**: The common term for many different traditions of [Neopagan](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Neopaganism) Witchcraft, also known as "the craft."   
  
**[Willard, Frances (1839-1898)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=84)**: Frances Willard was a Christian social activist who promoted [temperance](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Temperance), women's suffrage, labor reform and home-centered family life. She became involved in the Women's Christian Temperance Union (WCTU) in 1874 when she began preaching at daily temperance meetings in Chicago, and she eventually became WCTU president in 1879 (see [Temperance Movement](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Temperance%20Movement)). In her later life, she promoted Christian socialism, making her a forerunner of the [Social Gospel Movement](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Social%20Gospel). For more information on Frances Willard, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=84).   
  
**[Williams, Roger (1603-1683)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=3)**: Roger Williams was a [theologian](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Theologian), advocate for the separation of civil and church authority, and founder of Rhode Island. For more information on Roger Williams and his role in American history, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=3).   
  
**[Winthrop, John (1588-1649)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=24)**: John Winthrop was the first governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony. He was famous for describing the colony as a "city on a hill." For more information on John Winthrop, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=24).   
  
**[Witherspoon, John (1723-1794)](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=93)**: John Witherspoon was an influential [Presbyterian](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/family-trees?F=91) [minister](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Minister) in Colonial America. For more information on John Witherspoon, [click here](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/history/timelines/entry?etype=5&eid=93).   
  
**World Religion**: The broadest categorization of [religious affiliation](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Religious%20Affiliation). Examples of world religions include: [Christianity](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Christianity), [Judaism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Judaism), [Islam](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Islam), [Buddhism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Buddhism), and [Hinduism](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Hinduism).   
  
**Worship (Christianity)**: The public and ritual honor given to God in the name of [Jesus Christ](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Jesus%20Christ). It often consists of words ( [prayers](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Prayer) and other ritual formulas) and [sacred](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sacred) acts (see [sacrament](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Sacrament)). [Protestant](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Protestantism) churches tend to stress the verbal aspect of Christian worship over sacramental activity. [Catholic](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/groups?D=708) and [Orthodox](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=89) churches place a larger emphasis on the sacraments (Smith and Green 1995: 260).   
  
**Worship Style**: The types of activities that occur within the context of [worship](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Worship%20(Christianity)) services in a given religious group. Some worship styles are more [liturgical](https://www.thearda.com/research/religion-dictionary#Liturgy) (e.g., Catholic Mass), and some are more spontaneous (e.g., [Pentecostal](https://www.thearda.com/us-religion/group-profiles/families?F=94) services).
